subject: Spatial autocorrelation in the SPDE approach

messages.author: 2165994880cf93e8
messages.subject: Spatial autocorrelation in the SPDE approach
parts:
Good day,

I am new to INLA and thinking about applying the SPDE approach to my point referenced epidemiological data. I would like to ask you a general question about how spatial autocorrelation is taken into account in the SPDE approach (I read the SPDE tutorial and Lindgren et al 2011 paper but still find it difficult to understand).

Than you in advance.

Best regards,
Nicola

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Spatial autocorrelation in the SPDE approach
parts:
Hi Nicola,

Are you familiar with other computational methods for dealing with spatial autocorrelation? For example direct use of a covariance model? The spde method in inla is a more computationally efficient alternative for solving the same problem for a specific family of covariances, namely the Matern family of covariances. This means that from a modelling point of view, the spde method is equivalent (up to some approximation differences) to several other spatial statistics methods, so if you're familiar with any of those that might help to explain it.  If you haven't done any spatial statistics at all, you may need to read more of the fundamental literature. Since you're doing epidemiology, the new book by Blangiardo and Cameletti may be a good place to look, since it does precisely that, using inla and SPDEs.

Book link:
https://books.google.co.uk/books?id=--HuBgAAQBAJ&dq=blangiardo+Cameletti&lr=&source=gbs_navlinks_s

Finn

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Spatial autocorrelation in the SPDE approach
parts:
On 5 Aug 2016, at 10:08, Nic Smith <nic.jon...@gmail.com> wrote:
Did you mean "autocovariate model" when you wrote "direct use of a covariance model"?

Autocovariance, yes.  But in my view there is a vital distinction between "model" and "computational method"; most of the the stationary SPDE models we use have the same covariance functions as _any_ other method that works with Matérn covariance models. It's not the models that are different, it's the computational methods that are different. Indeed, the triple interpretation of covariances/differential operators/power spectra is often used within a single modelling/estimation/prediction problem, since the different interpretations of the same model are useful for different things.

I will read this book, thank you once again for your help.

Best regards, 
Nicola
